source.text: The 108 Prostrations of Repentance chanted with 108 bows in Korean Buddhism: a ritual text built on the repentance before the 35 Buddhas in the Sutra of Determined Vinaya and the names of the 53 Buddhas in the Sutra of the Two Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata
source.license: Original text: traditional liturgy, public domain
source.translationLicense: English translation and commentary: newly made by Sutra Box from its own Korean version (based on an AI draft, still being reviewed and refined)

bp01.heading: Verse of Refuge
bp01.plain: To the Buddha, who cherishes beings with great kindness and compassion, saves all living things with great joy and equanimity, and is adorned with a holy form and radiant light, we bow with utmost sincerity, offering our lives.
bp01.commentary: Opening the 108 prostrations, this praises the Buddha's four immeasurable minds (kindness, compassion, joy and equanimity). The first bow is made with this verse.

bp15.heading: Refuge in the Vajra Master and the Three Jewels
bp15.plain: I take refuge in the great master, firm as a diamond. I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, I take refuge in the Sangha.
bp15.commentary: The vajra master is the great teacher, indestructible as a diamond: the Buddha and the teachers who passed on the Dharma. Then one takes refuge in the Buddha, Dharma and Sangha. Bow once per line, two bows in all.

bp02.heading: Aspiration
bp02.plain: I now set my heart not to seek for myself the blessings of humans and heavenly beings, nor the stages of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas or bodhisattvas of provisional teachings. Relying only on the supreme vehicle, I raise the mind of awakening, wishing to attain supreme awakening at once together with all beings throughout the Dharma realm.
bp02.commentary: First the reason for bowing is made clear: not to pray for blessings or for one's own comfort, but to awaken together with all beings. Only bows made with this mind become repentance.

bp03.heading: Refuge in the Three Jewels
bp03.plain: I take refuge in all the Buddhas throughout the whole of space in the ten directions. I take refuge in all the honored teachings throughout the whole of space in the ten directions. I take refuge in all the wise and holy Sangha throughout the whole of space in the ten directions.
bp03.commentary: Bow once per line, three times. The repentance service proper opens by taking refuge in the Three Jewels that fill the universe to its edges.

bp16.heading: The Ten Names of the Tathāgata
bp16.plain: With utmost sincerity I give my life and bow to the Buddha who bears the ten names: Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened, Complete in Wisdom and Conduct, Well Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Tamer of People, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One.
bp16.commentary: These are the ten names for the Buddha: one who comes from truth (Tathāgata), worthy of offerings, rightly and fully knowing, complete in wisdom and conduct, well gone, knowing the whole world, unsurpassed, skilled at guiding people, teacher of gods and humans, the awakened one, honored by the world. Next, one bows to each of the fifty-three and thirty-five Buddhas in turn.

bp07.heading: The Fifty-Three Buddhas (1), from Universal Light Buddha
bp07.plain: I take refuge in Universal Light Buddha, Universal Brightness Buddha, Universal Purity Buddha, Tamālapattra Sandalwood Fragrance Buddha, Sandalwood Light Buddha, Maṇi Banner Buddha, Joyful Treasury Maṇi Jewel Heap Buddha, Great Vigor Buddha Whom All the World Rejoices to See, Maṇi Banner Lamp Light Buddha, Wisdom Torch Illuminating Buddha, Ocean of Virtue Light Buddha, Diamond-Firm Universally Scattering Golden Light Buddha, and Great Strong Vigor Courageous Buddha.
bp07.commentary: The fifty-three Buddhas come from the Sutra of the Two Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata. They are the first of the thousand Buddhas of the past Adorned Kalpa; hearing and revering their names is said to remove grave wrongs.

bp08.heading: The Fifty-Three Buddhas (2), from Great Compassion Light Buddha
bp08.plain: I take refuge in Great Compassion Light Buddha, King of Loving Power Buddha, Treasury of Love Buddha, Sandalwood Cave Adorned Victory Buddha, Wise and Good Leader Buddha, Good Intention Buddha, Vast Adornment King Buddha, Golden Flower Light Buddha, Jewel Canopy Illuminating Space Sovereign Power King Buddha, Space Jewel Flower Light Buddha, Lapis Adornment King Buddha, Universally Manifesting Form Light Buddha, and Unmoving Wisdom Light Buddha.
bp08.commentary: Each Buddha's name holds a virtue of its own. Bowing while calling the name is also a way of engraving that virtue in the heart.

bp09.heading: The Fifty-Three Buddhas (3), from Subduer of All Māras Buddha
bp09.plain: I take refuge in King Who Subdues All Māras Buddha, Brilliant Talent Buddha, Victorious Wisdom Buddha, Maitreya Sage Light Buddha, Quiet Moon Voice Wondrous Honored Wisdom King Buddha, World-Purifying Light Buddha, Supreme King of the Dragon Lineage Buddha, Sun and Moon Light Buddha, Sun and Moon Pearl Light Buddha, Wisdom Banner Victorious King Buddha, Lion's Roar Sovereign Power King Buddha, Wondrous Voice Victory Buddha, Ever-Shining Banner Buddha, and Lamp Watching the World Buddha.
bp09.commentary: As the bows go on the body tires, but if the mind gathers on each name, the bowing itself becomes meditation.

bp10.heading: The Fifty-Three Buddhas (4), from Wisdom Majesty Lamp King Buddha
bp10.plain: I take refuge in Wisdom Majesty Lamp King Buddha, Dharma Victory King Buddha, Sumeru Light Buddha, Sumanā Flower Light Buddha, Udumbara Flower Supreme King Buddha, Great Wisdom Power King Buddha, Akṣobhya Joyful Light Buddha, Boundless Voice King Buddha, Talent Light Buddha, Golden Sea Light Buddha, Mountain-and-Sea Wisdom Sovereign Penetration King Buddha, Great Penetrating Light Buddha, and King Ever Full of All Dharmas Buddha.
bp10.commentary: The udumbara is a legendary flower said to bloom once in three thousand years, a metaphor for how rare it is to meet a Buddha. After bowing to the last of the fifty-three Buddhas, one reads the text of repentance.

bp04.heading: The Thirty-Five Buddhas (1), from Our Original Teacher Śākyamuni
bp04.plain: I take refuge in our original teacher Śākyamuni Buddha, Indestructible Diamond Buddha, Jewel Light Buddha, Honored King of Dragons Buddha, Army of Vigor Buddha, Joy of Vigor Buddha, Jewel Fire Buddha, Jewel Moonlight Buddha, Manifesting No Delusion Buddha, Jewel Moon Buddha, Stainless Buddha, and Free of Stains Buddha.
bp04.commentary: These are the thirty-five Buddhas of the Sutra of Determined Vinaya. Repenting before them is said to purify even grave wrongs, so they have long been invoked in repentance prayer. Bow once for each name.

bp05.heading: The Thirty-Five Buddhas (2), from Courageous Giving Buddha
bp05.plain: I take refuge in Courageous Giving Buddha, Pure Buddha, Pure Giving Buddha, Varuṇa Buddha, Water Deity Buddha, Firm Virtue Buddha, Sandalwood Merit Buddha, Boundless Handful of Light Buddha, Light Virtue Buddha, Sorrowless Virtue Buddha, Nārāyaṇa Buddha, and Flower of Merit Buddha.
bp05.commentary: Varuṇa is taken to be a transliteration of the name of the water god Varuṇa. Nārāyaṇa comes from the name of a god of mighty strength.

bp06.heading: The Thirty-Five Buddhas (3), from Lotus Light Playful Powers Buddha
bp06.plain: I take refuge in Lotus Light Playing in Spiritual Powers Buddha, Merit of Wealth Buddha, Mindful of Virtue Buddha, Merit of Good Name Buddha, Red Flame Banner King Buddha, Merit of Good Walking Buddha, Victorious in Battle Buddha, Good Walking Buddha, Merit of All-Around Adornment Buddha, Walking on Jewel Flowers Buddha, and Sāla Tree King Dwelling Well on a Jewel Lotus Buddha.
bp06.commentary: These are the last of the thirty-five Buddhas. "Victorious in battle" means victory not over others but over one's own afflictions.

bp17.heading: Amitābha, Whose Body Is the Dharma Realm
bp17.plain: With utmost sincerity I give my life and bow to Amitābha Buddha, whose body is the whole Dharma realm.
bp17.commentary: The last (97th) bow to the Buddhas' names. "Whose body is the Dharma realm" means one who takes the whole Dharma realm as his body. Then, reading the repentance and dedication texts, one makes eleven more bows to complete 108.

bp11.heading: Repentance
bp11.plain: O Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, who ever dwell in all these worlds, keep me in your compassion. In this life or in past lives, since beginningless birth and death, all the wrongs I have done, whether I did them myself, made others do them, or rejoiced at seeing them done; taking things belonging to stupas, monks or the Sangha of the four directions, whether myself, through others, or rejoicing at seeing it; the five heinous deeds, whether myself, through others, or rejoicing at seeing them; the ten unwholesome paths, whether myself, through others, or rejoicing at seeing them; all the wrongs, hidden or not hidden, for which I should fall into the hells, the realms of hungry ghosts and animals, other evil realms, remote and lowly places and among barbarians: all of these I now repent.
bp11.commentary: The repentance is broad and honest. It owns as one's own fault not only what one did directly, but what one had others do and even what one was glad to see others do. This is the repentance of the thirty-five Buddhas from the Sutra of Determined Vinaya.

bp12.heading: Dedication
bp12.plain: Now may all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, bear witness and remember me. Again I say before the Buddhas: in this life or in other lives, whatever roots of goodness I have, from giving, from keeping the pure precepts, even from giving a handful of food to an animal, from pure conduct, from helping beings, from cultivating awakening, and from supreme wisdom, I gather them all, count and weigh them, and dedicate them all to supreme, perfect awakening. Just as the Buddhas of the past, future and present have dedicated their merit, so do I dedicate mine.
bp12.commentary: After repenting of wrongs, one dedicates every good deed to awakening. Even a small kindness like giving a handful of food to an animal is not left out. Six bows for the repentance text, four for the dedication and one for the verse that follows make eleven, completing 108.

bp13.heading: Verse of Repentance
bp13.plain: I repent of all wrongs, rejoice in all blessings, and by the merit of requesting the Buddhas to teach, may I attain supreme wisdom. The Buddhas of past, future and present are the most holy among beings; to that boundless ocean of merit I now bow, offering my life.
bp13.commentary: A verse that holds repentance, rejoicing (sharing joy in others' goodness), requesting the teaching, and dedication in four lines. The 108 prostrations end with the last bow.

bp14.heading: Mantra of Repentance
bp14.meaning: Oṃ, to all Buddhas and to the bodhisattvas who seek awakening, svāhā
bp14.commentary: The same repentance mantra found in the Thousand Hands Sutra. Chant it three times after finishing the 108 prostrations and the repentance text.
bp14.plain: A mantra of repentance before all Buddhas and bodhisattvas. It is chanted for its sound rather than translated.

four-immeasurables.definition: The four boundless minds: kindness that gives happiness, compassion that eases suffering, joy that rejoices in others' happiness, and equanimity that is impartial to all.

anuttara-bodhi.definition: Supreme, right and complete awakening: the awakening of a Buddha.

namo.definition: A transliteration meaning "I take refuge, I revere with my life." Said before a Buddha's name.

three-jewels.definition: The three treasures of Buddhism: the Buddha, the Dharma (teaching) and the Sangha (community of practitioners).

amitabha.definition: The Buddha of the Western Land of Bliss: the Buddha of boundless light and boundless life.

five-heinous.definition: Five grave wrongs said to lead to the Avīci hell: killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an arhat, drawing a Buddha's blood, and splitting the Sangha.

ten-unwholesome.definition: Ten harmful actions: killing, stealing and sexual misconduct by body; lying, idle talk, divisive and harsh speech by speech; greed, anger and delusion by mind.

parinamana.definition: Turning the merit one has made toward awakening or toward other beings, sharing it with them.

mantra.definition: The true words of Buddhas and bodhisattvas, chanted in their original sound rather than translated.

ten-epithets.definition: Ten names expressing the Buddha's virtues: Tathāgata, Worthy of Offerings, Perfectly Enlightened, Complete in Wisdom and Conduct, Well Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed, Tamer of People, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One.
